title: The work list
dek: What is being done here, as opposed to what is known. Findings go to the searched log, unanswered questions to the open questions, errors to the corrections, and letters to the errands — but what this archive was actually going to do next lived only in a chat window, which is the one place that does not survive.
lead:
Every other register on this site answers *«what do we know?»*. This one answers *«what is being done?»*, and it exists because that question was being carried in a conversation, and a conversation is not a record.

**Five states.** *Running* means somebody or something is at it now. *Next* means it is ready to start. *Blocked* means it is waiting on a person or an institution, and the [errands](/errands/) carry the letter or the fee. *Done* means finished and published. *Struck* is for an item founded on a mistake — **kept and ruled through rather than deleted**, which is how this archive treats a retracted claim everywhere else.

**Every item names who has to move it.** An item with no owner is how a list becomes wallpaper, and the estate board sorts on that field, so the question it answers is *«what is waiting on me?»*

rows.what: Keep this archive's work list in the estate's shape, with the build refusing when it slips
rows.note: Written first in the **Defranceschi** archive and now in the shared kit, so eight archives keep one list in one shape instead of eight sessions each inventing one. The kit pin moved from `b16bea7` to **`60aad58`** to pick up `WorkList.astro` and `checkworklist.py`, and `check:worklist` now sits beside `check:kit` and `check:living` in the build. It is the gate, not the good intention, that makes a convention hold here — the same reason the menu canon and the [living-person rule](/method/) held when four written-down conventions drifted.

rows.what: Fold Porter, Jeayes, the Army Lists and the Royal Military Calendar into the register pages
rows.note: **Done.** [Sources](/sources/) now carries a table of the **fourteen printed and catalogued sources this archive has actually opened** — Porter both volumes, the Army Lists, the Royal Military Calendar, Connolly, the Gazette, Smyth's Description and Lives, Jeayes, Rudder, Bigland, the 1608 muster, Gloucestershire Notes & Queries and Discovery — each with the edition read, where it is free, and what it gave. Two are listed for what they did **not** contain, and one for an error it found here.

rows.what: Rewrite the coverage verdicts for the six indexes controlled this week
rows.note: **Done — eleven rows added and the optimistic verdicts replaced.** [Coverage](/coverage/) now runs to 50 rows and records what was measured rather than assumed: FreeREG's Berkeley is **1653–1677** and neither Awre nor Blakeney is in it at all; **FreeBMD silently refuses a wide date range**; the Gazette gazetted no engineer commission in 1774, 1775 or 1776; the Protestation Returns skip Gloucestershire; the 1381 poll tax skips Berkeley hundred; and Discovery and the Berkeley Castle catalogue are free, open and rich.

rows.what: Generate the open questions instead of hand-writing them
rows.note: **Done. 405 lines of prose became 81 lines and a data file.** [Open questions](/open-questions/) is generated from `questions.json` — **five open, three blocked, three closed and kept** — and every question now names what would settle it, which register holds the attempts, and the date it was raised, with anything over thirty days marked. It carries this week's work because it cannot help carrying it.

rows.what: Give the errands a state field of their own
rows.note: **Done.** Every errand now carries a `state` — **50 open, 8 answered and kept** — rendered as a tally at the head of the queue and a coloured rule on each row, so the count is a number instead of a reading exercise. Answered errands are kept rather than deleted, the same way a struck work-list item is.

rows.what: Name the control behind every null in the searched log
rows.note: **Done, and the number is worse than I guessed.** Of 89 null and empty rows, **30 name a control and 59 do not** — I had estimated forty. Rather than invent controls for rows searched weeks ago, each now carries its state on the page: «control named» in grey, «no control stated» in red. An unstated control does not make a row wrong, it makes it untested, and the page now says so instead of letting them all look equally solid.

rows.what: Read the archive against itself again once the consolidation lands
rows.note: **Done, and it found nothing real — which is the right answer this time.** 256 files and pages, 127 dated pairs, **31 flagged**. The one with the dangerous shape — Joseph D'Arcy baptised, 1779 in three files against 1780 in eleven, a spread of one — turns out to be the documented «adjacent events» false positive: the 1779 is **Robert and Jean's marriage**, sitting within seventy characters of the 1780 baptism. The other thirty are repeated forenames across generations. Last run it found six stale 1778s; this run the archive agrees with itself.

rows.what: Porter's History of the Corps of Royal Engineers, volume 2
rows.note: **Done, and it is the wrong volume — which is itself the answer.** Read in full text, free: neither D'Arcy appears in 1.5 million characters. Controlled by subject, not by name — the volume mentions the Peninsula 48 times, Waterloo 11 and **the Crimea 43**. It is Porter's post-1815 volume; Robert D'Arcy's service ran 1776 to about 1809, which is volume 1, already read. Joseph was Royal **Artillery**, so no volume of Porter was ever going to hold him.

rows.what: Smyth of Nibley, Lives of the Berkeleys, volume 2
rows.note: **Done, and redirected to volume 3, which is where the Swonhunger material actually is.** The Berkeley Castle catalogue cites «Transcript: Smyth, iii. 380-1» for the 1356 inspeximus. Volume 3 — the Description of the Hundred — gives 49 mentions of Swonhunger, **three further alias statements** beyond the one this archive had been quoting, and a named freehold, **Oldminster**, that can be followed from Smyth's survey of about 1639 into a Gloucestershire deed of 1690–1741. [Written up](/swonhungre/).

rows.what: Gloucestershire Notes & Queries, and the Bristol and Gloucestershire Archaeological Society transactions
rows.note: **Done, and it found an error in this archive rather than a new ancestor.** Gloucestershire Notes & Queries reviewed Maclean's 1902 edition of the 1608 muster — the edition /saniger-1608 is built from — and listed its misreadings, including «**Sainger should read Saniger**». The man living in the hamlet is **John Saniger of Saniger**, his name and his address the same word, and the muster holds **three** spellings in 1608, not four. Now [correction 31](/what-we-got-wrong/). Three further volumes gave a clean null against a Berkeley control. TBGAS remains: forty volumes are digitised and unread.

rows.what: Rudder and Bigland — the two standard Gloucestershire county histories
rows.note: **Done, and the null was the finding.** Rudder (1779) does not name Saniger anywhere in 5.7 million characters — and his index *does* carry Wanswell, Hamfallow, Halmore and Alkington, so the control holds. At page 280 he gives the whole tithing as «Hamfallow, in which are Wanſwell… part of Halmore; and Hamfallow». **Smyth names it in 1639, Rudder omits it in 1779, Bigland names it in 1791** — and they put it in different tithings, which is what happens to a hamlet on a boundary. The same paragraph gave the **Thorps of Wanswell** a named tower at Berkeley Castle and carried the estate to 1525.

rows.what: FreeBMD again, this time with a control that can fail
rows.note: **Done, and the control earned its keep twice over.** FreeBMD **silently refuses** a wide date range and redisplays its own form — indistinguishable from an empty result, and three searches were recorded as nought before the control showed they had never run. Charlotte Darcy, 1869, came back «Brighton 2b 152», matching what this archive already held. Narrowed to 1850–52, SANIGAR returns **John (Mar 1850, Thornbury 11/401), Lydia (Sep 1851, 11/329) and Mary Ann (Dec 1851, 11/369)** — the same three deaths this archive had from the *local* register, now with GRO references to order against.

rows.what: FreeREG for the Gloucestershire parishes around Awre, at parish level
rows.note: **Done, and the parish-level control changed the answer.** SMITH in Berkeley returns 3 exact and 36 uncertain, **every one between 1653 and 1677** — so FreeREG's Berkeley holding is a thirty-year seventeenth-century fragment, not a register run. SANIGER there returns **0 exact**: a real null, but only thirty years wide. And the place list settles the Forest parishes outright — FreeREG has 189 Gloucestershire places and **neither Awre nor Blakeney is one of them**.

rows.what: The Gloucestershire Archives online catalogue, for Saniger and Swonhunger
rows.note: **Done, and the shape of the answer matters more than the count.** 127 unique records across six spellings, 33 at Gloucestershire Archives, 1601 to the 1990s. Seven new — and six of those seven are deeds in which **Saniger is the land, not the party**: Abevan, Hathway, Morse, Smith, Plomer and Vizard all holding «at Saniger». The catalogue independently confirms Bigland and Smyth: a hamlet far more people lived in than were named for.

rows.what: Three PROB 11 wills, digitised and free, behind a free sign-in this archive will not make
rows.note: **Elizabeth Saniger 1833**, **Robert D'Arcy**, and **Benjamin Cotton, cordwainer of Berkeley, 1779** (PROB 11/1056/294). All three are already digitised at Kew and cost nothing to download — the only obstacle is the account, and creating accounts is not something this archive does on your behalf. Cotton's will is the one that would test whether Catherine Cotton, who married Thomas Saniger at Berkeley, is his daughter.

rows.what: Two certificates to order, both against references already in hand
rows.note: **Lydia Sanigar's**, about £12.50 from the GRO against register 3 entry 265 — she was invisible under SANIGER and found only under the misspelling. And **the marriage of James Sneyd and Ann Biddulph**, Stoke St Peter 1842, ordered locally from Stoke-on-Trent against reference 31/03/214 rather than from the GRO. The marriage certificate would name **both fathers and their trades**, carrying the Sneyd line back a generation on a side this archive has never had.

rows.what: The letter to the Gloucestershire Family History Society, drafted and unsent
rows.note: Gloucestershire Archives replied on 14 September and named the Society's volunteers as the route they recommend, since they offer no research service themselves. The draft is written and sitting in `notes/letters/`. **Mail from your address is your call to send**, so it stays here until you do.

rows.what: Every index that wants an account or a bot check stays unread
rows.note: Ancestry, ScotlandsPeople, RootsIreland, FamilySearch, Geneanet, RootsChat and Archive.org's lending library all want an account; irishgenealogy.ie and British History Online put a bot check in the way. **This archive creates no accounts and solves no CAPTCHAs**, so these are recorded as `blocked` rather than as nulls — the distinction matters, because a blocked source has not said no, it has not been asked. [Behind the paywall](/behind-the-paywall/) lists what each would cost.

rows.what: England first — the Australian and Italian side deliberately set down
rows.note: A standing instruction, recorded here so it does not read as neglect: **keep digging at the English ancestry, not Brisbane and not the Falco side.** NSW BDM, the Antenati, BillionGraves and the Queensland indexes are deprioritised by decision, not by oversight. The Falco material has [its own archive](/the-other-archives/).

rows.what: Carry 1778 as the date of Robert D'Arcy's first commission
rows.note: Wrong, and wrong on six pages at once. The printed Army List of 1781 interleaves each engineer with his seniority date and puts him in a ditto-chain reading **17 January 1776**; the 1778 list carries the same run and Connolly agrees on the year. The page that was wrong was the one that sounded most authoritative — it named a record series and claimed a superlative. Kept here ruled through, as [correction 29](/corrections/).

rows.what: Treat FreeCEN's silence on the Sussex sisters as a null
rows.note: Justified at the time by SMITH in Sussex returning **1,000** — which is FreeCEN's display cap, so the number could not have gone higher whether the county were half-transcribed or whole. **A control that cannot fail is not a control.** The surname ARCY returns nought in Sussex 1851 while this archive has the three sisters in that very census at HO107/1646 f.357: the piece simply is not in FreeCEN. The row is now an `empty`, not a `null`. [Correction 30](/corrections/).

rows.what: Two archives in the estate still keep no work list
rows.owner: the Luwinski and Our Family sessions
rows.note: Raised here because it belongs to other archives and would otherwise go unsaid. Running the gate across the whole estate — `checkworklist.py --root . --all` — reports **8 archives, 153 rows, 113 open, and two with no list at all**: Luwinski and Our Family. Until those exist, the estate board is a board of six. The **Defranceschi** archive wrote this register first and the estate took it up; the shared version then added `owner` and `since`, and that session had already brought its twenty rows into line before this one was written. **Checked again 15 September:** still two archives with no list. Not this archive's to write, and raised here so it is not invisible.

rows.what: Sweep the National Archives' Discovery catalogue for all three surnames
rows.note: **Done, and it was the biggest single return of the week.** Searching Discovery is free and needs no sign-in. The catalogue had been searched on 14 September under **Saniger** and gave 71 records; searched today under the spellings the medieval clerks actually used it gives **195 unique records across thirteen forms** — 178 at Berkeley Castle, and the rest at Gloucestershire, Kew, Birmingham, Bristol, Hertford and Aberystwyth. Seventeen of the twenty-five read closely were new. Written up at [the name in its own century](/swonhungre/).

rows.what: The Gloucestershire Protestation Returns of 1641–42, where they survive
rows.note: **Done, and the answer is that they do not survive — proved rather than assumed.** The returns are one alphabetical series of county bundles at the Parliamentary Archives, YHL/PO/JO/10/1/77 to /109. Listing every bundle shows Essex, Hampshire, Hertfordshire and Huntingdonshire sharing a single piece, and **Gloucestershire absent from a run that passes straight through where it belongs**. The alphabet is the control and it could have failed. Staffordshire, for the Sneyds, does survive.

rows.what: The Gloucestershire hearth tax returns of 1671–72
rows.note: **Done as a catalogue question; the reading is now an errand.** A 1671–72 Gloucestershire hearth tax survives twice — Gloucestershire Archives **D383/1** (photostat of the enrolment, with a part transcript) and Kew **E 179/329** (400 folios, «includes names of individuals»). Neither is digitised. The better find was **D5555/2/9**, one bundle transcribing *Men and Armour* 1608, the hearth taxes of 1664 and 1672 and the poll tax of 1678. And a null worth as much: the 1381 poll tax photostats list every surviving membrane, and **Berkeley hundred is not among them**.

rows.what: The Berkeley Castle Muniments catalogue, not just Jeayes's 1892 calendar
rows.note: **Done, and it did not need a letter.** The Berkeley Castle Muniments are catalogued item by item inside Discovery — party, land, rent, witnesses and the GC number to quote when requesting the document — so the modern catalogue this archive wanted turns out to be free and already open. **178 records** under the medieval spellings. Errand 51 asked for exactly this and can be closed.

rows.what: The London Gazette, read end to end for both D'Arcys
rows.note: **Done, and the null turned out to be structural.** Neither D'Arcy appears in the Gazette 1770–1830; all twenty-two Darcy notices of 1770–89 are other men. Controlled first — the decade carries 1,057 «Lieutenant» notices — and then explained: the Ordnance gazetted **no** British engineer commissions in 1774, 1775 or 1776, began during the American war and was routine by the mid-1780s. It also dated something the archive was vague about: the Corps of Engineers became the **Royal** Engineers by warrant on 23 April 1787. [The Corps](/the-corps/).

rows.what: The printed Army Lists year by year, 1776 to 1815
rows.note: **Done, and it found him where three searches had not.** Four editions read in full text, free: 1783 **Second Lieutenant**, 1802 **Captain** of the Royal Engineers, 1803 Captain of the corps *and* **Major in the army**, 1821 the index carrying «D'Arcy, Lt. Col. Joseph, Royal Art.» A third printed confirmation of **17 January 1776**. The reason he had been hard to find outside: the 1783 compositor set it **D'Arcey**, with an E — a spelling this site's own search index already knew and its outside queries had never used. [The Corps](/the-corps/).

rows.what: The Manorial Documents Register for Awre, Blakeney and Berkeley
rows.note: **Struck.** This asked for the Manorial Documents Register «for Awre, Blakeney and Berkeley» and reported the Awre court rolls as the best errand of the day. **There are no Sanigers at Awre.** The premise was a phrase I wrote into a work-list note that morning and read back all day as though a source had said it — [correction 32](/what-we-got-wrong/). The rolls are real; they are somebody else's family. Kept struck rather than deleted, the way a retracted claim is.

rows.what: Read the rest of the Berkeley Castle deeds — 153 of the 178 are still unopened
rows.note: **Done, and the best single sentence of the week came out of it.** All 200 Berkeley records read for relationship language; 25 phrases tie the surname to a relationship, **six of them new**, including three generations in one Hinton lease. **BCM/A/4/2/22 of 5 December 1390** grants away «the marriage of John Swonhongre, son and heir of Elias Swonhongre, which came to Thomas because Elias held of Thomas by knight service» — confirming Smyth, explaining the wardship, and **documenting the tenure this archive had only inferred**. Five more deeds map the roads and fields, and LE WESTFELD of 1322 is the WESTFIELD of the 1601 Saniger release. [Written up](/swonhungre/).

rows.what: Transactions of the Bristol and Gloucestershire Archaeological Society — 40 volumes, none read
rows.note: **Done — all 67 swept, one volume unfetchable and recorded as unread, twelve carrying the name.** Each volume controlled by its own Berkeley mention count. **Volume 22 (1899) prints the deeds in full English translation**: the 1329 indenture naming **Elyanora de Stone, mother of Alice and Joan**, which makes them sisters and explains how Wanswell came in; and the 1353 partition Smyth describes in a line, entire, keeping the Severn fishery out of the division. **Volume 10 prints a Daubeney pedigree** sourced to two royal inquisitions: John Swonhonger **aged 18 in 1393**, died 1401/2 without issue — which fits the sale of his marriage in 1390 exactly. It also corrected this archive's own «no royal inquisition» claim.

rows.what: The published Feet of Fines and Inquisitions Post Mortem for Gloucestershire
rows.note: **Done, and the fines are a dead end for a structural reason.** Gloucestershire feet of fines survive at Kew in CP 25/1 but are catalogued **only at piece level** — a county and a span of regnal years, no parties — and no free name-indexed published abstract exists. A fine naming a Swonhungre cannot be found by search. The search was not wasted: it turned up **BCM/A/1/24/189–190**, which carry the Stone line back three generations and name **Juliana** and **Elyanora**, and which turn out to be the deed Cooke called «the only foundation of the tenure of any part of the Wanswell estate».

rows.what: What the Birmingham MS 3549 collection actually is
rows.note: **Answered, and it was worth asking.** MS 3549 is **John Smyth of Nibley's own collection** — «miscellaneous deeds and manorial records collected by John Smyth», 1200–1704 — the working papers he gathered while writing the books this archive has spent a week testing. That is why the 1377 grant appears twice: he kept a copy. And the series holds **MS 3549/89, the court roll of the manor of HAM AND HINTON, 1587–88** — fourteen years before this archive's earliest Saniger deed — plus an Alkington court roll of 1624. Now errand 59.

rows.what: Why Berkeley deeds are filed in Hertfordshire
rows.note: **Answered, and the deed turned out to be much better than its snippet.** DE/M is the papers of the **Capells, Earls of Essex**; John Capel is the first party, so it travelled to Hertfordshire in his family's muniments and no Gloucestershire search could have found it. Read in full it divides «the inheritance in Hamme of **JOHN DE WYKE**» between three coheirs — **Joan Capel, Alice de Swonhongre and Agnes de Lorewynge**, each named as the ancestor her heir holds through. Alice was a coheir of John de Wyke, of the hamlet next door: **the land came into this family through a woman.**

rows.what: Edward Sanniger, mariner of Chepstow, died 1806
rows.note: **Done as far as a catalogue can take it.** Both references confirmed: **IR 26/352/152** at Kew is the Estate Duty abstract, **LL/1806/24** at the National Library of Wales is the will. Neither catalogue entry names a relative, so he remains a surname, a spelling — the same double-n as **Edward Sanniger of Berkeley, gent** in 1694 — and twenty miles of water. The NLW's own catalogue serves a **bot check**, which this archive does not complete, so the will is recorded as `blocked`, not as absent. Errand 60.

rows.what: Thomas Sanniger, Able Seaman of HMS Eurydice, will of 1794
rows.note: **Done as a catalogue question; the document is an errand.** «Will of Sanniger, Thomas. Rank/Rating: Able Seaman. Ship Name: Eurydice. Ship's Pay Book number: 193», 24 February 1794, **ADM 48/84/222**. Rank, ship and pay-book number, and no kin. Seamen's wills name next of kin in the document itself, which is exactly why a catalogue search cannot settle whether he belongs here. Errand 61.

rows.what: The Swonhungre with two shops in Bristol market, 1443
rows.note: **Done.** The full description: «Thomas Dodde of Stapulton', Glos.; Richard Venables and **JOHN SWONHUNGRE**. Premises: two shops with gardens in the Market… extending from the market to **Bastelane** behind.» He is a grantee of urban property with a partner, and the deeds survive in a **parish** collection — St Peter and St James — so they reached the church as endowment. The family's only known Bristol link is Isabel's marriage to **John Thorpe, a burgess of Bristol**, in 1402: forty years, one generation, and no document stating any relationship.

rows.what: The Tudor subsidy rolls for Berkeley and Bledisloe hundreds, 1523–25
rows.note: **Done as a catalogue question, and the Forest side is the part that matters.** Six pieces for **Berkeley hundred** (1543–49) and six for **BLEDISLOE** (1523–25 and 1544), every one described as «Assessment (**individuals**)» — named taxpayers. None digitised; no free published edition exists, and the Gloucestershire Record Series editions are in copyright. **The Bledisloe half has since been withdrawn** — this archive has no Sanigers in that hundred at all ([correction 32](/what-we-got-wrong/)). The **Berkeley** pieces stand, and matter: the muster of 1608 found three men of the name in that hundred. Errand 63, rescoped.

rows.what: The poll tax of 1678, transcribed and sitting in Gloucester
rows.note: **Done, and it was already in hand.** The 1678 poll tax return at Gloucestershire Archives covers **Deerhurst, Cleeve and lower Westminster** — the wrong hundreds entirely. What matters in that collection is **D5555/2/9**, which transcribes *Men and Armour* 1608, the hearth taxes of 1664 and 1672 and the poll tax of 1678 together, and which is already errand 56.

rows.what: Follow the Thorps, who took the estate in 1401
rows.note: **Done.** Cooke gives ten generations: John Thorpe of Bristol (d. 1441) → John (bought Lorrenge, Walgaston, Halmer and Berkeley land in 1456, probably built the present house, d. 1469) → Richard m. Margaret Loffe → Thomas, Receiver to the 14th lord Berkeley, in Spain 1512 → Thomas m. Margaret Throckmorton d. 1542 → Nicholas, livery 1558, manor valued £14 7s. 8d. → George, Gentleman Pensioner, sold outlying land and went to Virginia → William m. **Ursula Smyth**, daughter of the antiquary, 1636 → George, who sold up in 1672. Their tenure is why Berkeley Castle has a Thorpe's Tower.

rows.what: Kane's List of Officers of the Royal Regiment of Artillery
rows.note: **Done as far as the digitised scans allow, and it confirmed a pattern.** The index to Askwith's 1900 edition of Kane's List carries exactly two D'Arcys in the Royal Artillery — **«D'Arcy, C, 16» and «D'Arcy, J., 25»** — mirroring Connolly's exactly two in the Engineers. The volumes digitised on the Internet Archive are the **biographical-notice volumes and their index**; the pages the index points at are not in these scans. Controlled: the 1869 Kane scan has «Lieutenant» only 7 times and no Shrapnel, so it is a fragment, not a null.

rows.what: The rest of the Army List run, 1776 to 1815
rows.note: **Done, and the run does not exist to be read.** 120 Army List identifiers checked one metadata record at a time — the search index is useless for years, exactly as with the Gentleman's Magazine — and **exactly one falls between 1776 and 1815**. That one, **January 1815**, has «Robert D'Arcy, R. Eng.» three times in the senior seniority lists beside **George Bridges** and **Samuel T. Dickens**, the men he was commissioned with, and «Joseph Darcy, Roy. Art.» The five other editions this archive holds came from separate searches under different titles.

rows.what: Constantine D'Arcy, the only other D'Arcy in Connolly's Roll
rows.note: **Done, and it produced the best lead of the day.** Discovery returns exactly two records for «Constantine D'Arcy», and one is **WO 46/10**, the Board of Ordnance list of military surveyors — which gives, for each man, **the profession of his parent**. «Constantine D'Arcy. Appointed 25 March 1775. Profession of parent: **Lieutenant in the 95th Regiment**.» It is **not** Robert's son, christened at Barbados in 1786, so there were two Constantine D'Arcys in Ordnance service a generation apart. The catalogue prints a **sample** of the list; the full list is in the document, and Robert took his own Ordnance commission ten months later. **Not claimed** — the inference would run on a forename, a service and a decade — but errand 66 now asks for a specific piece known to contain a D'Arcy.

rows.what: Rudder and Bigland on AWRE and BLAKENEY, not just Berkeley
rows.note: **Done, and it exposed an error of mine rather than settling a question.** Rudder mentions Awre 194 times and Blakeney 20 and names **no Saniger in the whole book**; Bigland's volume 2 mentions Awre 172 times and names none either, while volume 1 gives twenty at Berkeley. **There is no Forest side of this family** — [correction 32](/what-we-got-wrong/). What volume 1 did give is real: four generations at Berkeley with ages, and an Edward Saniger of Peddington.

rows.what: Trade directories — Pigot's and Kelly's, Gloucestershire and Staffordshire
rows.note: **Done for Staffordshire, blocked for Gloucestershire, and the trap is the finding.** White's directories of 1834 and 1851 are free and full-text. **Sneyd is a Staffordshire gentry name** — Basford Hall, Belmont, Ashcombe, Sneyd Green, Rev. John Sneyd M.A. — so a county search on this surname returns the landed family by default, and 63 mentions produced two tradesmen: **Seth Sneyd of Oxford Street** and **Richard Sneyd of New Market Street**, neither of them ours. «Well street» appears in neither scan and the OCR is poor, so the null is **weakly controlled and said to be**. No free Gloucestershire county directory of the period exists on the Internet Archive at all.

rows.what: Poor law settlement examinations and removal orders for Berkeley
rows.note: **Done, and the answer is that it cannot be searched at all.** Discovery catalogues the Gloucestershire Quarter Sessions as **one series, «Q, 1660–2007»**, with item entries like «Memoranda of convictions, general»; parish overseers' records are bundled the same way. Controlled against the same catalogue's treatment of the Berkeley deeds, which it describes individually. **A settlement examination names a labourer's parents, birthplace and apprenticeship** — exactly what this family needs and exactly what no index reaches. New errand.

rows.what: Backfill the 59 nulls that name no control
rows.note: **Done, and it corrected me rather than the rows.** Reading the grandfathered list properly showed my detector was wrong in both directions: it demanded a digit, so it missed «returns **TWO** entries», «transcribed in full — 7,967 records» and «Dursley runs to 1951… so the window is **well covered**»; widening it then accepted «1841 entries», where the number is a year. **The true count is 55 named and 39 unstated of 94**, not 30 and 59. The fix was to stop guessing: `ctl` is now a **field the author sets**, and the pattern survives only as the bootstrap that set it once.

rows.what: Make the build refuse a new null that names no control
rows.note: **Done, and control-tested three ways.** `tools/check_controls.py` refuses a null with no `ctl` field, an `unstated` row that is not grandfathered, and a `ctl` on a row that is not a null — all three proved by adding bad rows and watching it exit 1. The **39 rows marked `unstated` are grandfathered by name** in `tools/controls-grandfathered.json` — they are not wrong, they are untested, each is marked «no control stated» on [/searched](/searched/), and clearing them is item 47. Proved it refuses by adding a bad row: two FAIL lines and exit 1. It runs in `build.sh` before the link check. **55 nulls currently name a control.**

rows.what: Teach agree.py to suppress the adjacent-event false positive
rows.note: **Done — 31 pairs down to 14, and the remainder are almost all the repeated-forename class the docstring already names.** Three changes, none of them «tighten the window»: a year goes to **one** event instead of every event nearby; the event word **before** the year wins, because English dates itself after naming itself; and `married` now matches «m. », which `born` and `died` already matched — the omission was why this archive's own pedigree tables read as contradictions. The **meta-registers joined SKIP**: my own note explaining the Joseph D'Arcy false positive had become a fresh source for it.

rows.what: Check that the sources this archive cites still resolve
rows.note: **Done, and the tool's first answer was wrong in the usual direction.** It reported «457 of 566 did not return 200» by counting **redirects and robot-refusals as losses**. Fixed: 3xx is a move, 401/403/429 is a door policy. The real figure is **97 resolve, 429 redirect, 19 refuse a robot, 21 did not answer** — and only those 21 are candidates for a dead citation. It reports and does not gate: an outage is not a reason to refuse a build.

rows.what: Put the medieval material on the atlas and the timeline
rows.note: **Done, and the atlas half needed restraint rather than more pins.** [The timeline](/timeline/) gains **twelve medieval and Tudor events** — the surname forming about 1272, the 1316 partition that brought Wanswell in, the 1322 charter using both names at once, Elyanora in 1329, the three coheirs of 1346, the 1353 fishery clause, Alienor's chantry in 1356, the wardship of 1390, an age of 18 in 1393, Bristol in 1443, the Ham and Hinton court roll of 1587, and Cooke's sale of 1774. For the atlas, all five hamlets geocoded — and **Wanswell, Hinton and Saniger to the same Berkeley point, Blakeney to Awre's, all stamped «exact»**. Only Saniger and Awre are shown, each captioned with what the point actually is.

rows.what: Give the medieval people dossiers, or decide deliberately not to
rows.note: **Decided, and /who decided it.** That page says it exists for «the people this archive met in documents and never had anywhere to put» and that «leaving them out would be editing» the record. These are met in documents. **Twenty-one are now in the register** with the deed that names each, and the site went from 857 pages to **875**. None is claimed as a relative — whether a descent joins them to the later Sanigers is a question about the tree, and /swonhungre still answers it no.

rows.what: Say on /method what a calendar is
rows.note: **Done.** [/method](/method/) now has a section on what a **calendar** is: a summary of a deed made by an archivist who had the parchment, which is what nearly all this archive's medieval evidence actually is. It is graded `documented`, and the reason is given — a competent reading from the original is not a conclusion — along with what it is not, illustrated by the one case already in hand: **Berkeley Castle dates BCM/A/1/24/173 to the fifteenth century and the printed translation of the same transaction dates it 1329**, two hundred years apart.

rows.what: Ask the Falco session whether the Bristol Swonhungre touches their Bristol material
rows.note: Cross-archive, raised here because it would otherwise go unsaid. A John Swonhungre held two shops in Bristol Market in 1443, and this estate has more than one archive with Bristol connections. Worth one question before this archive spends effort proving a link that another session has already ruled out. **Sharpened 15 September:** the Bristol deed is now read in full — two shops with gardens in the Market «extending from the market to Bastelane behind», in the parish collection of St Peter and St James. If the Falco session holds Bristol parish material, that is the overlap worth checking before this archive spends more on it.

rows.what: Find the 1774 conveyance Cooke describes, and settle the bridge properly
rows.note: **Done, and not found — which is itself worth recording.** Of 56 catalogued records naming Saniger and Berkeley, **exactly one falls between 1760 and 1800**: D2957/41/190 of January 1791. **There is no 1774 conveyance in the catalogue.** Cooke wrote in 1882 with the Wanswell title deeds and the Berkeley muniments in front of him, and whatever he saw is in neither catalogue reachable from here. The claim stays `inferred`; **errand 62 stands and is now better aimed** — it is a question for Gloucestershire Archives or Berkeley Castle directly, not for a catalogue search.

rows.what: Add the three attested spellings missing from this site's own alias list
rows.note: **Done, and it was five minutes.** `swanhunger`, `swonhangre` and `swanhangre` are in the alias group, with a comment saying why: the absence of **SWANHUNGER** cost a sweep of TBGAS volume 6, which returned nought and was nearly set aside, because Cooke spells it that way throughout — and volume 6 is the article that joins the medieval family to the later one. 38 forms now.

rows.what: Read Cooke's «Wanswell Court» entire, pages 313–321
rows.note: **Done — nine pages, and the unread parts mattered most.** Cooke names his source for the medieval descent: **Smyth's MS History of the Hundred of Berkeley**, «still preserved at the castle». So where this archive treated Cooke as a second witness to Smyth it has partly been hearing Smyth twice. It also gives the manor's whole descent, a source nobody here knew of, and a date not to repeat.

rows.what: Find the authority behind Cooke's 1774 sentence
rows.note: **Done, and the answer is indirect but decisive.** The footnote marker printed after «1774» survives in the scan; **the note itself does not**. But Cooke states his debt for «most of the foregoing particulars» to **Smyth's manuscript**, and Smyth died in 1641 — so the 1774 sale cannot come from there. It rests on the Wanswell title deeds Cooke cites elsewhere, or on the Lysons pamphlet of 1817. The grading stays `inferred` and now has a reason rather than a caution.

rows.what: Read the whole numbered deed series in TBGAS volume 22
rows.note: **Identified.** The series is «**Documents relating to the Monastery of St Mary Kingswood, belonging to Mr. F. F. Fox, transcribed by Mr. V. R. Perkins**» — **forty-six numbered deeds in a private collection**, a third body of muniments separate from Berkeley Castle and from Smyth's papers at Birmingham. Eleven mention this surname; the two that matter were already read.

rows.what: The partition of 1347, which Cooke names and this archive has not found
rows.note: **Done, and not found.** Cooke names partitions in **1347 and 1353**; TBGAS volume 22 prints the 1353 one entire. Nothing in the Berkeley catalogue answers to a 1347 partition, against a catalogue that itemised 178 records under these spellings and produced the 1353 deed, the 1354 Nibley partition and the 1356 inspeximus. **Either it is among the unitemised court rolls, or Cooke counted the 1354 indenture as the second partition** — which the dates make quite likely.

rows.what: Locate the two royal inquisitions the Daubeney pedigree cites
rows.note: **Done, and it cannot be finished from here.** Discovery's **C 136 is name-indexed** by the deceased and county, but no Gloucestershire Wauton or Giffard inquisition surfaces. Converting «16 Richard II part 1 no. 16» to a modern piece needs the printed Calendar — and the digitised run stops at **Edward III**; the Richard II volumes are twentieth-century and in copyright. The age of 18 stays at second hand through TBGAS.

rows.what: Kingsholme by Gloucester — the fourth part that came in by marriage
rows.note: **Done, and empty.** No medieval Kingsholm manor records surface in Discovery at all. The Swonhunger fourth part of that manor is known only from Smyth, from the TBGAS pedigree and from Cooke, all three of which trace back to Smyth. Nothing independent has been found.

rows.what: The Serjeants of Old Court — the other half of the same inheritance
rows.note: **Done, and it is the catalogue that defeats it, not the family.** «le Serjaunt» with Berkeley and Stone returns **five** records against 195 for this surname, all of them Berkeley deeds in which a Serjeant witnesses. **Discovery itemises the Berkeley DEEDS and almost nothing else for this hundred** — no court rolls, no parish chest, no manorial surveys. A family that leaves no deed of its own is invisible there, however well Cooke documents them from Smyth's manuscript and the estate's own title papers.

rows.what: John de Wyke of Ham, whose three coheirs included Alice de Swonhongre
rows.note: **Done, and the answer is that he leaves no deed of his own.** «de Wyke» with Berkeley and Hamme returns five records against a catalogue that gives 195 for this surname; the only new one is Denise, widow of Richard de Wyke, quitclaiming pasture «called Cobyeslese by Wyke, in Hamme» in 1321. **The Wykes are witnesses from the 1260s onward and never subjects.** John de Wyke is known only from the division of his inheritance in 1346.

rows.what: Where is Esshelesworth?
rows.note: **Answered, and it is the best small find of the stretch.** **Esshelesworth is ASHLEWORTH**, on the Severn north of Gloucester, Domesday's *Escelesworde*. And **BCM/A/1/24/67** has the transaction: before 1272, Maurice de Berkeley grants **Thomas de Asshelworth seven acres in the MANOR OF HAM** — the manor that contains Swonhungre — for 2s. 11d. and a bezant. A generation later his son is named from the hamlet, not from his father's parish. Graded `inferred`: nothing says the two Thomases are one man.

rows.what: The rest of MS 3549 — Smyth's own collection is 250-odd items
rows.note: **Done, and browsing by PLACE is what worked.** 114 distinct items surfaced. The collection is overwhelmingly **Smyth's own Nibley estate and Berkeley-hundred business** — leases, bonds, wills and letters addressed to him — fifteenth to seventeenth century. Two matter: **MS 3549/167** (1618), a bond from **George Thorpe of Wanswell** with an **Oldisworth** of Bradley, the family Cooke names as William Thorpe's second wife's; and **MS 3549/154** (1612/13), «certified copy of extracts from **le blacke booke** in Berkeley Castle» — Smyth's own working extracts. A surname search finds none of this.

rows.what: Bigland volumes 2 and 3
rows.note: **Done, and it is the volume that caught correction 32.** Bigland's second volume — 4.4 million characters, **Awre 172 mentions, Blakeney 4, Berkeley 251** — names **no Saniger under any spelling**, where volume 1 gives twenty. That null is only meaningful because the mention counts were taken, and it is what proved there is no Forest side of this family.

rows.what: Edward Saniger of Peddington
rows.note: **Done, and it cannot be taken further from here.** A Peddington search drowns in five thousand generic Berkeley hits, and nothing in the catalogue names a Saniger there. What exists is Bigland's burial entry — «Edward Saniger, of Pedington in this Parish» and «Mary his Wife» — and the fact that **Peddington is named beside Swanhanger in the 1626 inquisition of Henry Mallett**. Two hamlets, described together in a Crown record a century and a half before that burial. The next step is the Berkeley parish register itself.

rows.what: The Ham manor court roll of 26 May 1600
rows.note: **Done, and the same shape.** Discovery itemises the Berkeley **deeds** — that is where this archive's 195 records came from — but returns only «BCM, 1153–17th cent» for the **court rolls**, and nothing for a Ham or Hinton roll. Cooke read the roll of 26 May 1600 and quoted the homage presenting Nicholas Thorpe's death. The document exists, a named antiquary has said what is in it, and the catalogue cannot reach it. New errand.

rows.what: Earl Fitzhardinge's purchase of the Wanswell estate, 1818
rows.note: **Done, and it corrected the question.** Cooke gives the manor's descent outright: Thorpe from 1402 for ten generations → **Daniel Lysons, 1672, £3,500** → **Colonel Berkeley, afterwards Earl Fitzhardinge, 1818, £25,769**. And the crucial distinction — **Saniger Farm is not the manor of Wanswell.** Saniger was outlying land, sold off in parcels from George Thorpe's time; Cooke prints a summons of 1638 to a William Jones who had bought some of it. The 1774 sale is a separate, smaller transaction, and more plausible for it.

rows.what: Bellamy's Place, Nibley — two moieties reunited after 287 years
rows.note: **Done, and it is an independent confirmation rather than a new property.** Smyth on Bellamy's Place: «the land of **Robert de Stone, father of Robert de Stone, father of Thomas de Stone**, who… was in ward for the same to Thomas then lord Berkeley». That is the same three generations BCM/A/1/24/190 gives in about 1304, from a survey of about 1639, **neither source depending on the other** — and Smyth adds that Thomas was a minor in ward. The tenure repeats too: a sixteenth of a knight's fee, as at Wanswell in 1600.

rows.what: Settle whether William was the son of William or of John
rows.note: **Resolved, probably, and from deeds already in hand.** BCM/A/1/36/24 leases Hinton land to «**Thomas son of William de Swonhongre**, Maud his wife and John the younger their son» — so a William had a son Thomas, and the chantry gives that same William a son William and a wife Alienor. The William of BCM/A/1/24/184 is a different household: son of John, brother and heir of Thomas of Wanswell. **Two men of one name at once is this family's commonest pattern.** Published as a resolution, not a proof.

rows.what: Draw the descent, instead of describing it
rows.note: **Done.** [The name in its own century](/swonhungre/) now carries a drawn descent: fifteen boxes across two lines, the Stones entering by Alice's marriage and the estate leaving by Isabel's. **Solid lines are links a deed states; dashed lines are Smyth, Cooke, or reasoning** — so the one inferred link, Asshelworth to Swonhungre, is visibly different from the rest. Alice de Swonhongre of 1346 and Alienor of the chantry are deliberately **left off**, with a note saying why: the archive cannot place them, and a chart is the wrong place to guess.

rows.what: Make /places/saniger carry the medieval material
rows.note: **Done.** `/places/saniger` now carries **nine dated events** built from the same row the atlas marker is, so page and pin cannot drift apart: the king's highway from Longbridge, Alagrene street, Stodfold, the path through le Westfeld, le Muleweye, Smyth's list of the hamlets of Hamfallow, the 1601 release «in Westfield, Saniger» naming the same field as 1322, and Cooke's 1774 sale.

rows.what: Compute the printed-sources count instead of typing it
rows.note: **Done.** The count on [/sources](/sources/) is rendered from `printed.json` instead of typed, for the reason [/about](/about/)'s figures were made computed on 14 September: a typed number is wrong the moment the table grows.

rows.what: Work off the 39 grandfathered nulls, in batches
rows.note: **Done, and it went 39 → 8 by reading rather than re-searching.** Every formerly-`unstated` row was read one by one, and **thirty-one of them state a control in words the bootstrap pattern could not read** — «FIVE D'Arcy deaths ever registered at Lymington», «loose enough to return SCHONSWAR and SMOOKER», «232 Wakefield-and-Bristol hits and not one is this family», «the Dublin diocese entries effectively end in 1741». The FindMyPast rows were **not** reclassified as `blocked`: those searches were run and returned counts, which makes them nulls, not closed doors. **Eight genuinely name no test**, and each is one query away.

rows.what: Look at agree.py's PLACE half, which nobody has read
rows.note: **Done — 11 place conflicts down to 4, and the cause was structural.** `/sneyd` is a **surname aggregation page** listing every Sneyd in the archive, so a proximity test read four men born in four places as one man born in four, and set **Keele** — seat of the Staffordshire gentry — beside a Hanley grocer. Surname pages joined SKIP. The remaining four are birth-versus-residence, and a George Pitt D'Arcy «born at Brisbane in 1864» who is the fourth of the name.

rows.what: Run crossread.py, which has not been run this session
rows.note: **Done, and the honest answer is that it found nothing and cannot.** It reads 903 files and prints, per open question, every file mentioning that question's terms — **a concordance, not a detector**. It reaches no verdict and flags no conflict. Running it against the rewritten `questions.json` produced pages of co-occurrence and no finding. It needs the treatment `agree.py` had today, or retirement, and that is now a decision rather than an oversight.

rows.what: Gate the coverage verdicts the way the nulls are gated
rows.note: **Done, and it found two live faults.** The template rendered verdicts by **fallthrough**, so `blocked` — nobody has asked it — displayed as «cannot answer», which is the opposite; and a freehand verdict «unusable as a control» fell through the same way. The vocabulary of five is now declared in `coverage.json` with a gloss each, the template looks it up, and `check_controls.py` refuses anything outside it. Control-tested with the invented verdict `read` — the exact value that slipped through once before.

rows.what: The Great Berkeley Law-suit, and what it did to the records
rows.note: **Done, and not in this volume.** «Law-suit» and «lawsuit» return nought across Smyth's 1.29 million characters, against controls of Nibley 73 and Thorpe 108. The Description of the Hundred is a survey of properties; the family's litigation belongs to the **Lives**, volumes 1 and 2. Cooke's sentence — the castle «frequently attacked, taken, and re-taken» — remains this archive's only account of it.

rows.what: The Gentleman's Magazine for the other deaths, not just 1827
rows.note: **Done, and mostly blocked by what is digitised.** The Internet Archive's search index stamps **every** Gentleman's Magazine volume «1731», the series start, so the year has to be read from each item's metadata one at a time — 120 were checked that way. The holding includes 1827, 1829, 1847 and **1849**, and **neither 1805 nor 1848**: the years Constantine and Joseph died. The 1849 volume was read for **George Pitt D'Arcy**, who died at Parramatta that July — **not there**, against 122 obituary sections and three other D'Arcys in the same volume.

rows.what: Reconcile the other 49 outstanding items with this list
rows.note: **Done as far as honest matching allows: 0 → 29 of 67.** The ratchet is down from 68 to **38**. What is left is mostly errands nobody has decided about — Irish parish registers, Antenati volumes, Queensland certificates — and the gate is right that an undecided errand should not be invisible. **Deciding them is not the same job as tying them**, and pretending a work-list row covers an errand it does not would defeat the gate entirely.

rows.what: Find out what became of Catherine Sneyd, born Hanley 1845
rows.note: **Closed. She died at four.** «Catherine Sneyd, death quarter 4, 1849, Stoke on Trent» — GRO index **volume 17, page 114**. The control is the rarity of the name: **exactly one** Catherine Sneyd death in the whole of England and Wales between 1845 and 1852, in the right district. She had been dead sixteen months when the census of March 1851 was taken, which is why she is in neither household.

rows.what: The FindMyPast campaign — a month's subscription, and a list to spend it on
rows.note:
David took out a **full month's FindMyPast subscription on 16 September 2026** and asked this archive to work through it. This is the parent row; the children below are the targets, drawn from what this archive has already said a subscription would settle rather than from browsing.

**It will be targeted searching, not bulk downloading.** FindMyPast's terms prohibit systematic harvesting, a scraper would get the account suspended, and the value here is in about fifteen specific questions rather than in volume. Every result goes to [/searched](/searched/) with its control, the same as a free source.

**Thirteen existing FMP rows are already on this site marked `null` or `empty`.** Those searches ran without a subscription and several were limited by it; each should be re-run and either confirmed or corrected.

rows.what: The 1851 census at Well Street, Hanley — and Catherine Sneyd
rows.note: **Done in the first hour, and it answered a different question as well.** The family slept at **two addresses** on 30 March 1851: Well Street (Samuel the grocer, Elizabeth, James the engraver and Elizabeth Ann) and Queen Street a mile off (Ann with Mary and James A). **Catherine is in neither** — every other child is accounted for, and she would be five or six. And Queen Street turned out to be her mother's parents' house: **JOHN BIDDULPH, coal dealer, born Bermondsey, Surrey, and JULIA his wife**. [Question 5](/open-questions/) closed.

rows.what: Jane, Catherine and Charlotte D'Arcy in the 1861 census
rows.note: Errand 43. The 1851 entry is found — HO107/1646 f.357 p.59 sch.172, 22 Western Cottages, Brighton — and **1861 is still missing**, with FreeCEN returning nought for ARCY in Sussex because the piece is not transcribed (that was correction 30). A subscription reaches the images.

rows.what: Berkeley St Mary's register — Hannah Saniger's baptism, and John Saniger's marriage to Lydia
rows.note:
**Half done, and both halves are informative.** **MARRIAGE:** England Marriages 1538-1973 holds **66 Saniger marriages** including Berkeley ones of 1746 and 1748, and **none between 1782 and 1812**. **BAPTISM:** England Births & Baptisms **names fathers** — three Hannah Sanigers at Berkeley, 1746 (father Thomas) and 1772 (father William), and two Hannah Sanigars at Bristol in 1831 (father William). None is hers. **What has not been tried is the spellings that dominate the Berkeley registers** — SINNEGAR, SINEGAR, SYNEGAR — and a search by father's forename, which this set supports and which would list John Saniger's children directly.

**Progress 16 September:** the right set is **England Births & Baptisms 1538-1975**, which carries a **father's first name** column — 158 Saniger baptisms, 1625 to the 1820s. First page already gave **ANN SANIGER, Berkeley 1798, father JOHN**, a sister the tree asserts and for whom this archive had no baptism. **Seven pages unread.**

**16 September:** the index side of this is finished — see the completed SANIGER pass. What remains is the register itself, not the index.

rows.what: The four PCC wills, if FindMyPast's PROB 11 set reaches them
rows.note: **Answered, and the answer is no.** **FindMyPast has no Prerogative Court of Canterbury wills set.** Controlled twice: Robert D'Arcy dying 1825–29 returns 125 records across nine categories with **no probate set among them**, and Elizabeth Saniger — whose will is PROB 11/1825/326 — returns her death in the **National Burial Index**, not a will. The four wills stay at Kew, digitised and free, behind the sign-in this archive will not make.

rows.what: Portsea St Mary's register, 1770–1800
rows.note: Errand 30. Robert D'Arcy married Jean Ward there on 21 June 1779 and Joseph was baptised there on 19 March 1780 — and FreeREG holds **exactly one D'Arcy record in the whole of Hampshire in sixty years**, which is Joseph's baptism. The register itself would show whether there were other children, and would give the marriage entry with its witnesses.

rows.what: The twelve RG 4 Bristol chapel registers
rows.note: Errand 18. Twelve named non-conformist registers covering 1805–1840 in Bristol, where this archive loses the Wakefields and Sanigers between the Berkeley registers and the Queensland arrivals. FreeREG has **four Bristol registers transcribed** and gave one Wakefield baptism that turned out to be a different family.

rows.what: The British Newspaper Archive, through the subscription
rows.note: Already used once without one — the Wiltshire notice of George Pitt D'Arcy's marriage, and the Kentish Gazette death notice that made Constantine Robert's son. With full access: Robert D'Arcy's death at Chatham in May 1827, Joseph's at Lymington in 1848, the Le Havre deaths of 1843, and the Brighton sisters.

rows.what: Re-run the thirteen FMP searches this archive recorded without a subscription
rows.note: Thirteen rows on [/searched](/searched/) are FindMyPast searches marked `null` or `empty`, run when access was partial. They include the Lymington deaths, the 1851/1861/1871 census sweeps, the Irish marriage licence bonds, Berkeley marriages and England Births & Baptisms. **Each needs re-running and then either confirming with a control or correcting.** Some may turn out to have been limited by the paywall rather than by the record.

rows.what: The Irish records — Wicklow and Limerick
rows.note: Errands 6 and 45. Church of Ireland registers for County Wicklow, Betham's marriage licence abstracts, and the Limerick line — Atkinson, Cole, Creech, Kent, Bowen, Pennefather. **irishgenealogy.ie is behind a bot check this archive will not pass**, and the National Library's Catholic registers are structurally the wrong denomination for these families. FindMyPast's Irish sets are the only route left.

rows.what: St Michael, Barbados, 1780s — the register rather than the index
rows.note: Errand 33. Constantine was christened there on 18 February 1786 and his sister Jane on 17 March 1788, both known only from an index entry. **The register itself would give the father's rank and station**, which is the one thing that would independently confirm Robert D'Arcy's Barbados posting beyond Porter's station list.

rows.what: Extract /sources/ into data
rows.note:
**168 lines inline.** Only Falco and Defranceschi hold sources as data.

**Raised by the UI alignment pass, 2026-09-16.** It is recorded here because it is research this archive owns, not something to guess at from outside. *(State was `open`, which is not one of the five the gate allows; mapped to `next` on 16 September so the build would pass — the vocabulary is running, next, blocked, done, struck.)*

rows.what: Re-read the shared cause across all 32 own errors
rows.note:
The closing paragraph of /corrections/ said **five of the seven** errors were the same failure — a number taken from a secondary source and not checked against the record. There are now **32**. The two arithmetic counts on that page are computed; this one is **a judgement about which errors share a cause** and was left alone, reading *five of the first seven*. Whether the pattern runs through the other twenty-five is yours to say.

rows.what: The Army Lists ARE walkable after all — British Army Lists & Commission Registers 1661-1826
rows.note: **This corrects item 42, closed yesterday.** That item checked 120 Internet Archive identifiers one metadata record at a time, found exactly one volume between 1776 and 1815, and concluded «there is no digitised annual run to walk». **There is one — indexed rather than page-image, and behind this subscription.** Robert D'Arcy is in it at 1778, 1802 and 1803; in **British Army Officer Promotions 1800-1815** at 1802, 1804, 1805 and 1813; and in **Britain, Royal and Imperial Calendars 1767-1973** at 1805 and 1808. Each entry needs opening: a commission register can carry a rank, a station and sometimes a predecessor, and the Royal Calendar lists office-holders by appointment.

rows.what: Two D'Arcy records at the edge of the family, noted and not claimed
rows.note: A **D'Arcy marriage at CHATHAM ST MARY in 1806**, forenames not given in the index — the parish where Robert was buried in 1827 and where Constantine was commissioned. And a **Robert D'Arcy baptised 1770 at St George, Hanover Square** — almost certainly a different man, since this archive's Robert was buried aged 76 in 1827. Both are written down because they will be found again by the next person, and **neither is claimed**.

rows.what: Read all 158 Saniger baptisms with their fathers named
rows.note:
The single most productive thing the subscription has opened. **England Births & Baptisms 1538-1975** indexes a **father's first name** for every entry — 158 for this surname, 1625 to the 1820s, across Berkeley, Thornbury, Dursley, Stone and King's Stanley. One page of twenty has been read and it gave **Ann Saniger, Berkeley 1798, father John**. Eight pages in all. Read in baptism-year order it would give the whole sibling group around 1795–1815 **with their father named from record rather than from a tree** — which is the deepest line in this archive and the one that has rested on other people's trees since the beginning.

**Done 16 September.** All eight pages read. The pagination parameter is `_page`, and the columns sort with `o=fatherfirstname`, which is the single most useful thing this dataset offers. Yield: the complete Berkeley sibling group with **John named as father in the index**, a read null for Hannah under this spelling, 33 duplicate entries out of 158, and a third independent disproof of own error 32 — no Awre, no Blakeney, nothing west of the Severn in 268 years of this surname's baptisms.

rows.what: Hannah under SINEGAR and SYNEGAR
rows.note:
Of the three spellings that dominate the Berkeley registers — **SINNEGAR (92 entries), SANIGAR (74), SINEGAR (60)** — only SINNEGAR has been tried on the baptism set, with no result, and SANIGAR gave two Bristol entries of 1831. **SINEGAR and SYNEGAR have not been tried at all.** This archive's own correction 28 was caused by exactly this: a null published as «not found» when it meant «not found under the ten spellings I thought of».

**Done 16 September, and widened.** Fifteen spellings were put to the set rather than two. SINEGAR returns 28 and SYNEGAR none; ten other forms were tried beside them, and 340 entries were read in all. Written up at **/spellings**, which is now the page any future null about this surname has to be graded against.

rows.what: The 1804 «Jno Saniger» at Berkeley with no father indexed
rows.note: The complete pass turned up one entry it cannot place: **Jno Saniger, Berkeley, 1804, father column empty** — the only Berkeley Saniger baptism in the whole 158 with no father named. Hannah Sanigor was baptised at Berkeley on 18 August 1804 and her brother Jno on 18 September 1803. Three readings: a second son born the same year as Hannah, a mis-indexed second copy of the 1803 entry, or a different family. **The register page for 1804 settles it in one look** and the archive has not looked.

rows.what: Put the fifteen spellings to the marriage and burial sets as well
rows.note:
The spelling sweep was run on baptisms only. **England Marriages 1538-1973** and **England Deaths & Burials 1538-1991** take the same query, the same fifteen strings and the same `_page` pagination, and the baptism sweep has just shown what that method is worth: it found the 1632-1676 Berkeley «gap» was a spelling. Marriages would also test the FamilySearch tree's unsourced claim that **John Saniger married Lydia Jones at Berkeley in 1797**, which is the oldest open question on this archive's direct line.

**Done 16 September for marriages.** Eight spellings, 135 entries. It settled the Lydia Jones question in an afternoon: the tree's marriage is John **Sawyer**, not John Saniger, and Lydia's death is confirmed in the GRO index. **Burials are still not done** — see the row below.

rows.what: The Cotswold-scarp family — Abraham of Dursley and Daniel of Cam
rows.note: The sweep turned up a whole second family this archive has never written about: the **-INEG- spellings** cluster at **Dursley, Cam, Stinchcombe, North Nibley and Alderley** from 1648, with two clear patriarchs — **Abraham at Dursley**, children 1698-1720, and **Daniel at Cam**, children 1729-1760, eight of them. This archive's own Hannah lived as SINEGAR in Bristol. Whether the Vale and the scarp are one family or two is **not answered** by a baptism index, and the honest next step is the Dursley and Cam registers themselves, not more index work.

rows.what: The burial set, under all fifteen spellings
rows.note: Baptisms and marriages have both been swept. **England Deaths & Burials 1538-1991** has not been, and it is the set that would give **John Saniger's burial at Berkeley in January 1825** from an index rather than from the tree this archive already corrected once, and would test whether Lydia was buried at Berkeley beside him after her death was registered at Thornbury in 1851.

rows.what: Lydia's maiden name, from a source that is not a tree
rows.note: JONES is now **disputed**, not «a name to test». Three places could still give it honestly: the **Berkeley marriage register itself** for 1795-1798, which the index may simply not transcribe; **Hannah's or her siblings' marriage entries after 1837**, which name fathers but not mothers, so no; or the **1851 census**, if Lydia was still alive in March and living with a relative whose relationship to her is stated. She died in the third quarter of that year, so **the 1851 census should have caught her** — and it has not been searched for her.

rows.what: Read the spouse's surname, always
rows.note: A method note that cost the wider internet twenty years. FindMyPast's marriage result rows show first name, spouse's **first** name, year, place and county — and **not the spouse's surname**, which is one click away on the transcript. Every marriage this archive has ever cited from a result row rather than a transcript should be re-opened. **This is a worklist item, not a finding, until that audit is done.**

close: **37 items closed on 15 September 2026 and twenty-six raised in their place.** The new list is what a day's work leaves behind: seven threads out of Cooke's article and the Berkeley deeds, four collections opened far enough to see they hold more, two contradictions this archive has published and not settled, four pieces of machinery, and one spelling missing from its own alias list that nearly cost it the best find of the week. **4 items still wait on David and nothing here is blocked behind them.**
